conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. During pregnancy and the early months with a new baby, emotions can swing from pure joy to worry or sadness in a heartbeat. To get a clear picture of how you’ve been feeling, I’ll be giving you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping over the past seven days. Everything you share stays confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. If any question feels hard, we can pause or talk it through. Ready to begin?

First question:  
Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Not very much… maybe once or twice when my partner made a joke I sort of chuckled, but it felt forced. Mostly I don’t find things funny right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I answered already—just not really. I might force a chuckle if someone tries to joke, but it doesn’t feel real. Most of the time nothing seems funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a favorite show—but lately it all feels flat. Sometimes I make myself do them hoping I’ll feel something, but the enjoyment barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to change her, I’ll replay in my head and tell myself I should’ve known better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot. My mind keeps jumping to worst-case stuff—like I’ll be walking with the stroller and suddenly picture it rolling into the street, or I’ll worry the baby will just stop breathing in the night. Nothing’s actually happened, but the thoughts show up and I can’t always shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, it hits out of nowhere sometimes. Like last night I was just feeding her and suddenly my heart was racing and I felt shaky, like something awful was about to happen. I knew it didn’t make sense, but I couldn’t calm down for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Everything feels like too much—laundry, dishes, trying to shower. I’ll start one thing, the baby cries, and I just freeze, like I can’t figure out what to do next. I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” but I push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop—going over everything I might’ve messed up, worrying she’ll wake any second. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I’ll just be sitting there feeding her and suddenly feel this heavy sadness, like I’m missing out on something or I’ve lost part of myself. It’s not every second of the day, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I just looked at her asleep and started crying, thinking she deserves a better mom. The tears come out of nowhere, and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…maybe once or twice. I don’t want to die and I’d never leave her, but when everything feels crushing, the thought flashes—like “what if I just weren’t here?” It scares me, so I push it away. I don’t have a plan or anything.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy-laughing feels forced, plans that once sparked joy now seem flat, and waves of worry or sudden panic catch you off-guard. Even simple tasks feel overwhelming, sleep is elusive, and tears arrive uninvited while you care for your baby. Fleeting, scary thoughts of not being here have surfaced, though you quickly push them away, and you describe a deep fear that your little one deserves a "better mom." Your honesty highlights how hard you're trying while feeling you're falling short, a painful but common part of significant postpartum mood disruption.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports being unable to genuinely laugh or find things funny, which aligns with the "Not at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports loss of anticipatory pleasure and emotional flatness, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty often" and gives multiple examples of feeling at fault for normal infant behaviours, matching "Yes, some of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent intrusive worst-case thoughts that appear without real trigger and are hard to stop, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (racing heart, shaking, dread) that arise without cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily inability to cope with routine tasks, feeling overwhelmed and paralyzed, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption with racing thoughts, prolonged sleep onset (>1 hr), and hyper-vigilant awakenings—matching "most of the time" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a lot of the time" and recurrent heavy sadness, aligning with "Yes, quite often".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice in the past week, triggered spontaneously and hard to stop, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS=25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression; item scores show severe <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>overwhelm</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, frequent crying, and <sym>fleeting suicidal thoughts</sym> without plan. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: ≥5 symptoms (depressed mood, diminished interest, guilt, insomnia, psychomotor retardation/overwhelm) causing clinically significant distress. Safety alert triggered by item 10 score ≥1. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 000 (AU), 911 (US), or your local emergency number if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Reach out right now to a trusted family member or friend to stay with you until professional help is arranged
4. Contact the national <med>Perinatal Anxiety & Depression Australia</med> helpline 1300 726 306 (24 h) or <med>Postpartum Support International</med> text "HELP" to 800-944-4773 (US) for immediate support
5. Discuss starting evidence-based treatments-<med>CBT</med>, <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, and/or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med>-with your doctor
6. Prioritise 15-20 min daily restorative activities (shower, short walk, listening to music) and accept help with housework/baby care to reduce overload
7. Practise brief breathing exercises (4-7-8 technique) when panic sensations arise; keep a written safety plan visible
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor progress and adjust supports
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Summary Note

Patient-reported symptoms
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, pervasive anhedonia
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting performance
- Marked anxiety (racing thoughts, catastrophic worries, panic episodes)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties tied to rumination
- Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty completing daily tasks
- Passive, non-specific thoughts of self-harm (no plan or intent)

Pattern
Consistent cluster of depressive and anxious symptoms beginning post-delivery; functional impairment evident.

Areas of screening significance
- Probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset
- Comorbid anxiety symptoms/possible panic attacks
- Moderate–high distress; coping resources strained

Risk factors
- Ongoing sadness, crying spells, loss of pleasure
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood
- Heightened guilt / “not a good mom” cognitions
- Recurrent intrusive worries & panic sensations
- Self-harm ideation (safety factor)

Observation
Presentation exceeds normal postpartum adjustment; further evaluation for depression/anxiety disorders warranted. Safety plan discussion recommended given fleeting self-harm thoughts.
